title: AI chips
summary: What an AI chip does all day, why memory limits it as often as math, and five ways to build one.

ideas.how: GPUs keep weights in HBM next door; SRAM chips keep them on the chip itself
a GPU uses thousands of simple cores instead of a few complex ones
spare cores route around manufacturing defects
AI chips drop what AI does not need and add more of what it does

tradeoffs.how: each halving of the number size halves the memory traffic
SRAM chips are fast but small; HBM holds whole models

measures.how: AI chips compete on it as much as on speed
the biggest difference between AI chips is often here

born: Deep learning takes off on GPUs in 2012.
then: Deep learning runs on GPUs; the transformer architecture comes in 2017.
The first AI chips: Google's TPU (revealed 2016) and GPUs used for deep learning.
Transformers (2017) scale up; models grow from millions to billions of parameters. Tensor cores (2017), TPUs and a wave of AI chip startups.
Large language models serve hundreds of millions of people.

challenges.title: Feed the beast
challenges.task: Serve a 70B model in FP8 on Rubin and raise the batch until the chip stops waiting for memory. Where does each user start to slow down?
challenges.hint: Raise the batch a step at a time and watch chip utilization. Below 100%, the chip is waiting for memory.
challenges.why: With one user, every token reads all 70 GB of weights for very little math, so the chip waits for memory. Serving many users at once reuses each read, and somewhere between 512 and 724 users the math becomes the limit. Past that point, each user gets slower.

challenges.title: Sixteen answers
challenges.task: Predict how many cycles a 4 × 4 systolic array needs to finish all 16 results, then step through it one cycle at a time to check.
challenges.hint: Data enters the array one diagonal at a time. The last cell starts late and still needs all 4 steps.
challenges.why: A 4 × 4 systolic array needs 10 cycles, 3 × 4 − 2. The last numbers reach the far corner only after the first ones have crossed the array. Bigger arrays have the same fill-up delay, which is why they are fed long streams of work.

challenges.title: An assistant in your pocket
challenges.task: On the phone NPU, find the biggest model that fits on one chip and still answers at 20 tokens a second, faster than you can read.
challenges.hint: On a phone, memory bandwidth sets the speed. Try smaller numbers for each weight.
challenges.why: With 4-bit weights, a model of about 8 billion parameters fits on one phone chip at 20 tokens a second; with 8-bit weights, only about 4 billion. Phone AI depends on smaller numbers as much as on faster chips.

challenges.title: Four bits, despite outliers
challenges.task: With 1% outliers in the weights, fit a 70B model in under 40 GB and keep the signal-to-noise above 20 dB.
challenges.hint: Only 4-bit formats fit under 40 GB. Then try each way of scaling.
challenges.why: Only FP4 with one scale per block of 16 weights works: 39.4 GB and about 20.5 dB. With one scale for the whole tensor, a few large outliers stretch the scale and crush every small weight to zero. Small blocks keep each scale local, at the cost of half a bit per weight.

challenges.title: Read fast, write slow
challenges.task: On Rubin with a 70B model, find how long a prompt must be before reading it takes as long as writing a 270-token answer.
challenges.hint: Keep the answer at 270 tokens and lengthen the prompt until the time to first token is close to the time spent writing.
challenges.why: It takes a prompt of about 77,000 tokens. Reading the prompt works on all its tokens at once, so the chip computes at full speed; writing produces one token at a time and waits for memory each time. Per token, reading is about 280 times faster.

learn.plain: An AI chip is a giant multiplication machine. It runs fastest when its thousands of calculators stay busy, which means feeding them data quickly from memory and serving many people at once. All AI chips are giant calculators. The big difference is where they keep the numbers they work on: in memory chips next door (GPUs and TPUs), or spread through the chip itself (wafer-scale and SRAM designs). Keeping numbers closer is faster, but holds less.
learn.engineer: Decode is memory-bound: arithmetic intensity is about 2 × batch ÷ bytes per weight FLOP per byte, far below ridge points in the thousands. KV-cache reads add to weight traffic at long context. Standard tools include FP8 and FP4 quantization with block scaling, speculative decoding, continuous batching, paged KV caches, and splitting compute-bound prefill from bandwidth-bound decode onto different hardware, which NVIDIA's Rubin CPX targets. The design space has five main axes: compute density (MACs per mm²), memory hierarchy (HBM capacity versus on-chip SRAM bandwidth), programmability (SIMT cores versus compiler-scheduled systolic or dataflow execution), scale-up fabric (NVLink, ICI, UALink) and number formats (FP8 E4M3/E5M2, block-scaled MXFP4 and NVFP4). Decode rewards bandwidth per byte of model; prefill and training reward dense FLOPS and fabric bandwidth.

quiz.q: What do wafer-scale chips and SRAM-dataflow chips (LPUs) have in common?
options: They keep the model's data in on-chip SRAM, right next to the compute
quiz.why: On-chip SRAM gives enormous bandwidth but limited capacity, so these designs trade memory size for speed.

quiz.q: Why does block scaling make FP4 work much better?
options: It adds more bits to every number
Each small block of values gets its own scale, so a few outliers don't ruin the rest
It runs the chip at a higher clock
quiz.why: NVFP4 uses blocks of 16 and MXFP4 blocks of 32, costing only 0.25 to 0.5 extra bits per weight.

quiz.q: Why are prefill and decode increasingly run on different hardware?
options: Prefill is compute-bound while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound
quiz.why: Matching each phase to hardware built for its bottleneck, such as Rubin CPX for prefill and LPUs for decode, lowers cost and latency.
That is why AI chips devote most of their area to arrays of MAC units.

quiz.q: When generating text for a single user, an AI chip is usually limited by…
quiz.why: Every token requires reading all the weights, but only two operations per weight.

quiz.q: Why does serving many users at once (batching) help?
options: It reuses each weight read from memory for many users
It skips layers of the model
quiz.why: Batching raises arithmetic intensity, moving the workload toward the compute ceiling.
